Date: 2022-12-12
REMARKS
In view of the claim amendments below remarks, the Examiner is respectfully requested to reconsider the rejections. Applicant has filed an After Filing Consideration Pilot (AFCP) request, and invites the Examiner to contact the undersigned for an interview if appropriate.
Office Action Summary
Claims 19, 30, and 33 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as failing to set forth the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 34 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, 4th paragraph, as being of improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends.
Claims 16-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (a)(1) as being anticipated by Gillian et al., (US20170097413A1) (hereinafter "Gillian").
Claims 21 and 22 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Hauenstein et al., (US20170095181A1), (hereinafter "Hauenstein").
Claim 23 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Sun et al., (US20120203491A1) (hereinafter "Sun") and Komaromi et al., (US20160162256A1) (hereinafter "Komaromi").
Claim 24 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 16 above, and further in view of Attal et al., "Physical Human Activity Recognition Using Wearable Sensors" Sensors 2015, 15, 31314-31338, (hereinafter "Attal") and Eriksson et al., (US20170172467A1) (hereinafter "Eriksson").
Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 20 above, and further in view Kim et al., "Tracking a Moving Target with Multipole Doppler Sensors Using an Artificial Neural Network", IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium, June 9-15, pp. 1477-1480, (hereinafter "Kim") and Rogers, (US20170351827A1) (hereinafter "Rogers").
Claim 26 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 17 above, and further in view of Sun and Komaromi.
Claims 27-30 and 34 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Sun and in further view of Komaromi.
Claim 31 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Sun and Komaromi applied to claim 29 above, and further in view of Rogers.
Claim 32 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Sun, Komaromi, and Rodgers applied to claim 31 above, and further in view of Hauenstein.
Claim 33 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Sun, Komaromi, and Hauenstein.
Claim 35 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian, Sun, and Komaromi.
35 U.S.C. § 112(b)
Claims 19, 22, 30, and 33 have been amended to recite "worn by the user" rather than "worn with the user".
35 U.S.C. § 112(d)
It is respectfully submitted that claim 34 limits the subject matter from which it depends. Claim 27 recites "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user." Referring to FIG. 3B, this for example corresponds to the time during which pseudo sensor data 370 is provided because native sensor data 360A is not provided. Claim 34 recites "wherein the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived in response to an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is providing native sensor data for the user." Referring to FIG. 3B, this for example correspond to the beginning of native sensor data 360B, and the end of the derivation of the pseudo sensor data 370.
It might potentially in some examples be a contradiction if claim 34 recited "wherein the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived in response to an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user." However claims 27 and 34 are instead of the form do A when not B (claim 27) and do not A when B (claim 34), which is not a contradiction.
35 U.S.C. § 102/103
The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Sections 102 and 103, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2131 ("A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference."); MPEP 2143.03 ("All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art.").
1. Independent claims 16, 27, 35: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable
Independent claim 16 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable." Independent claims 27 and 35 have been amended similarly.
Support for this amendment is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 7, line 34 to page 8, line 17, and FIG. 3B.
Gillian paragraph [0043] describes "In this particular example, the sensors 118 include an accelerometer 202 and gyroscope 204. These and other motion and positional sensors, such as motion sensitive MEMS or global positioning systems (GPSs) (not shown), are configured to sense movement or orientation of the computing device 102. The accelerometer 202 or gyroscope 204 can sense movement or orientation of the device in any suitable aspect, such as in one-dimension, two-dimensions, three- dimensions, multi-axis, combined multi-axis, and the like. Alternately or additionally, positional sensor, such as a GPS, may indicate a distance traveled, rate of travel, or an absolute or relative position of the computing device 102. In some embodiments, the accelerometer 202 or gyroscope 204 enable computing device 102 to sense gesture inputs (e.g., a series of position and/or orientation changes) made when a user moves the computing device 102 in a particular way."
Gillian paragraph [0092] describes "At 606, the one or more reflection signals are transformed into radar data representations. The reflection signals may be transformed using any suitable signal processing, such as by performing a range-Doppler transform, range profile transform, micro-Doppler transform, I/Q transform, or spectrogram transform. Continuing the ongoing example, the radar sensor performs a range-Doppler transform to provide target velocity and direction information for the user's hand."
Gillian paragraph [0094] describes "At 610, a sensor is activated based on the radar feature. The sensor can be activated to provide supplemental data. In some cases, a sensor is selected for activation based on the radar feature or a type of the radar feature. For example, an RGB or infrared sensor can be activated to provide supplemental sensor data for a surface feature or motion feature. In other cases, an accelerometer or gyroscope can be activated to obtain supplemental data for a motion feature or position feature. In yet other cases, data may be received from a microphone or depth sensor to improve a detection feature. Continuing the ongoing example, the sensor fusion engine 110 activates the RGB sensor 220 of the laptop 102-5 to capture spatial information."
Sun paragraph [0035] describes "Thus, under this context (e.g., high physical activity), the system 100 stops collecting and/or processing data at the physiological sensor or sensors while the user is active. Using the context information collected at the first sensor or group of sensors (e.g., the accelerometer data) to stop data collection and/or processing at the second sensor or group of sensors enables the system 100 to: (1) save resources (e.g., battery life of the sensor), and (2) increase the accuracy of the sensor data analysis by avoiding collecting data when artifacts can reduce the quality of the data."
Komaromi paragraph [0015] describes "The action triggered is subject to the kind of wearable electronic device. However, for any wearable electronic device, one action may be to either power down or to switch to a stand-by mode if the output signal changes from a detected "on-body" state-i.e. the device is worn by a user-to an "off-body" state-i.e. the device is detected to no longer be worn. This action may support saving battery power which is important for wearable devices of all kind in view of a lack of a permanent power source. Hence, in one example, a hearing aid may be powered down when the hearing aid is determined to be-off-body-i.e. out of the ear of the user. The same may hold for earphones. Also glasses, watches, headphones or clothes with integrated electronics may no longer be supported by power in case an off-body state is detected. As said before, the action may be triggered in response to a change of the value of the output signal, or may be connected to presence of a state of the output signal."
Komaromi paragraph [0036] describes "In a different embodiment, the device comprises one or more further sensors which may, for example, be medical sensors. One or more of powering the sensor/s, evaluating, or logging of data from the further sensor/s preferably is stopped or paused in response to the device no longer being detected to be worn."
The Examiner stated on pages 16, 21, and 22 of the Office Action that Gillian, Sun, and Komaromi at the above-referenced excerpts (Gillian [0094], Sun [0035], Komaromi [0015] and [0036]) describes "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user."
However Gillian, Sun, and Komaromi do not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable. This is because Gillan at best describes deriving radar data representations, Sun at best describes stopping data collection and/or processing based on context, and Komaromi at best describes switching to a stand-by mode if an output signal changes from a detected "on-body" state-i.e. the device is worn by a user-to an "off-body" state.
The Examiner also applies the above-referenced excerpts (Gillian [0092] and [0043], Sun [0035], Komaromi [0015] and [0036]) on pages 13-14 of the Office Action to reject the aspect of claim 26, namely "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in part with a sensor, that generates the native sensor data representative of activity of the user, not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user."
In the Response to Arguments section of the Office Action, the Examiner stated on page 24 of the Office Action that "however nowhere in the claims does it specify the pseudo sensor data bridges this gap":
SVG
{EMBED HERE}
1.4 6.29
As amended, the claims now specify that the pseudo sensor data bridges the gap where the native sensor data is not provided, as the claims now recite wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable. This is not described by Gillian, Sun, or Komaromi.
Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable. Independent claims 16, 27, and 35, on the other hand, claim "wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.
2. Dependent claim 24: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the machine learning model is trained with training data comprising at least reference radio frequency based data and reference sensor data, the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity, wherein the machine learning model is trained using supervised training with the reference sensor data, and wherein the training comprises learning at least one relationship between the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data
Dependent claim 24 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the machine learning model is trained with training data comprising at least reference radio frequency based data and reference sensor data, the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity, wherein the machine learning model is trained using supervised training with the reference sensor data, and wherein the training comprises learning at least one relationship between the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data."
Support for this amendment is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 6, lines 28-30 ("In the example of FIG. 3A, the vertical line 390 represents a point in time during which the user 102 performs an activity. As shown at 390, the sensor data 202, 204, 206 indicates the activity at 210A-C, which corresponds in time to the RF based data activity 315A-B"), page 9, lines 20-23, page 11, lines 1-5, FIG. 2 in combination with FIG. 3A, FIG. 5A (hidden layer learned from reference sensor data 530 and reference RF based data 510), and FIG. 6 item 606.
Gillian paragraph [0073] describes "Any suitable type of algorithm can be used to extract a feature, such as machine-learning algorithms implemented by a machine- learning component (not shown) of the digital signal processor 126."
Gillian paragraph [0092] describes "At 606, the one or more reflection signals are transformed into radar data representations. The reflection signals may be transformed using any suitable signal processing, such as by performing a range-Doppler transform, range profile transform, micro-Doppler transform, l/Q transform, or spectrogram transform. Continuing the ongoing example, the radar sensor performs a range-Doppler transform to provide target velocity and direction information for the user's hand."
Gillian paragraph [0094] describes "At 610, a sensor is activated based on the radar feature. The sensor can be activated to provide supplemental data. In some cases, a sensor is selected for activation based on the radar feature or a type of the radar feature. For example, an RGB or infrared sensor can be activated to provide supplemental sensor data for a surface feature or motion feature. In other cases, an accelerometer or gyroscope can be activated to obtain supplemental data for a motion feature or position feature. In yet other cases, data may be received from a microphone or depth sensor to improve a detection feature. Continuing the ongoing example, the sensor fusion engine 110 activates the RGB sensor 220 of the laptop 102-5 to capture spatial information."
Attal section 3.2 describes "3.2 Classifiers":
In this study, a 10-fold cross validation procedure was used to create the training set and the test set. In the case of supervised approaches, the models were trained using the training set. In the test step, the estimated classes were compared to the true classes in order to compute the classification error rates. In the case of the unsupervised approaches, the models were trained using only the raw data without considering the labels. The labels were only used to evaluate the classification performances. In the test step, the classifiers outputs (estimated labels) were matched with the true labels in order to evaluate the classifier performances.
Eriksson paragraph [0040] describes "An activity type may be determined based, at least partly, on sensor data. This determining may take place when the activity is occurring, or afterwards, when analysing the sensor data. The activity type may be determined by device 110 or by a personal computer that has access to the sensor data, for example, or a server that is provided access to the sensor data. Where a server is given access to the sensor data, the sensor data may be anonymized. The determination of the activity type may comprise comparing the sensor data to reference data. The reference data may comprise reference datasets, each reference dataset being associated with an activity type. The determination may comprise determining the reference dataset that most resembles the sensor data, for example in a least-squares sense. Alternatively to the sensor data itself, a processed form of the sensor data may be compared to the reference data. The processed form may comprise, for example, a frequency spectrum obtained from the sensor data. Alternatively, the processed form may comprise a set of local minima and/or maxima from the sensor data time series. The determined activity type may be selected as the activity type associated with the reference dataset that most resembles the processed or original sensor data."
The Examiner stated on page 11 of the Office Action that the above-referenced excerpts (Gillian [0073], [0092], [0094], Attal Section 3.2, Eriksson [0040]) describes pre-amended claim 24.
However, the prior art does not disclose or suggest claim 24 as amended, because a) Eriksson at paragraph [0040] only describes reference datasets, but not "reference radio frequency based data... collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity." Eriksson gives no indication that the reference dataset is reference radio frequency based data (despite Gillian describing generally radar data), or that the reference data is collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity, as claimed by Applicant.
This is also because b) Attal and Eriksson do not describe "wherein the training comprises learning at least one relationship between the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data." In Attal, machine learning is used only to learn a relationship between sensor data and an activity. Refer to Attal Abstract ("classification techniques used to recognize human activities from wearable sensor data"). In Eriksson least squares is used to determine an activity type, comprising "determining the reference dataset that most resembles the sensor data" (refer to Eriksson paragraph [0040]), effectively comparing the reference dataset to the sensor data during an inference phase to determine the activity type, not during a training phase.
In contrast, Applicant's training phase comprising learning a relationship between one type of data (radio frequency data) and another type of data (sensor data) while both types of data are generated when a reference user is performing an activity.
Refer e.g. to Applicant's filed specification at page 6, lines 28-30 ("In the example of FIG.
3A, the vertical line 390 represents a point in time during which the user 102 performs an activity.
As shown at 390, the sensor data 202, 204, 206 indicates the activity at 210A-C, which corresponds in time to the RF based data activity 315A-B") and page 11, lines 3-5 ("Referring also to the example at FIG. 5A, the machine learning model 599 may iterate through the reference RF based data input 510 given the reference sensor data at the output 530 until the model 599 learns a hidden layer 540 configuration (e.g., a set of weights and/or other parameters)"). This is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art.
Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the machine learning model is trained with training data comprising at least reference radio frequency based data and reference sensor data, the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity, wherein the machine learning model is trained using supervised training with the reference sensor data, and wherein the training comprises learning at least one relationship between the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data. Dependent claim 24, on the other hand, claims "wherein the machine learning model is trained with training data comprising at least reference radio frequency based data and reference sensor data, the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data collected from at least one reference user performing at least one activity, wherein the machine learning model is trained using supervised training with the reference sensor data, and wherein the training comprises learning at least one relationship between the reference radio frequency based data and the reference sensor data." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, dependent claim 24 is patentable and should be allowed.
3. Dependent claim 34: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived in response to an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is providing native sensor data for the user
Dependent claim 34 claims:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived in response to an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is providing native sensor data for the user."
Gillian paragraph [0073] describes "As another example, consider a scenario in which the signal transformer 502 transforms the raw radar data into a measure of the target object's velocity over time. In turn, the feature abstractor 504 uses this information to identify a finger fast-tap motion by using a threshold value to compare the target object's velocity of acceleration to the threshold value, a slow- tap feature, and so forth. Any suitable type of algorithm can be used to extract a feature, such as machine-learning algorithms implemented by a machine-learning component (not shown) of the digital signal processor 126."
The Examiner stated on page 18 of the Office Action that Gillian at the above- referenced excerpt ([0073]) describes the aspect of claim 34.
However, Gillian does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived in response to an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is providing native sensor data for the user. Gillian at paragraph [0073] only describes identification of motion by comparing an object's velocity to a threshold (where the velocity is a result of a transformation of raw radar data), and using machine learning to extract a feature.
In contrast, Applicant describes no longer deriving the pseudo sensor data in response to an indication that the native sensor data is being provided. Referring to Applicant's FIG. 3B, this aspect relates to the end of 370 (no longer derive the pseudo sensor data) and the beginning of 360B (indication that native sensor data is being provided). Applicant's FIG. 3B is provided below to illustrate this aspect:
SVG
{EMBED HERE}
3.02 3.95
This aspect is not described by the prior art including Gillian. For this additional reason claim 34 is patentable.
4. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above
Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103. For example, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine the references to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above.
5. Other dependent claims
Though the other dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, including amended claim 31, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. Support for the amendment to claim 31 is found within the filed specification at page 4, lines 11-14, and page 12, lines 16-20. To expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.
Conclusion
The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
Respectfully submitted,
